title: Whipped Tallow Balm in Pear: My Weird Jar of Beef Fat That Actually Works
body:
Okay so I’m just gonna say it. I put beef fat on my face. I know. It sounds like something you’d do on a dare, or like, a weird historical reenactment thing. My first thought was literally “absolutely not.” But my skin was being such a jerk this spring—all dry and flaky but also weirdly oily?—and I was scrolling Etsy at like 1 AM, phone at 12%, and I saw this jar of Whipped Tallow Balm. The Pear scent one. And I don’t know, man. I was tired. I clicked buy. A beef tallow skincare product showed up at my door a couple weeks later and I just stared at it for a solid day before I even opened it.

My cat kept sniffing the box. Judging me, probably.

## How I Started Putting Tallow on My Skin

Look. I’ve tried everything. The fancy department store stuff that costs as much as my electric bill. The “clean” beauty creams that smell like a forest and do nothing. The drugstore lotions that just sit on top of my skin feeling gross. My elbows looked like a topographic map of the moon. So when this little jar arrived, I figured, how much worse could it be? The whole beef tallow for skin concept sounded medieval. But then I started poking around online, half out of curiosity, half to justify my weird purchase to myself.

Turns out, using animal fats on skin isn’t new. It’s ancient. My grandma probably would’ve just nodded and said “of course.” She had that kind of wisdom about using what you have. People have been using tallow balm for ages—for chapped hands, windburn, you name it. It’s just pure, rendered fat from grass-fed beef. And the science-y part that made me pause is this: the fatty acid profile in tallow is supposedly really close to the oils our own skin makes. Our sebum. So the idea is it doesn’t just coat your skin; it recognizes it. It gets absorbed. It’s like giving your skin something it actually knows how to use, instead of some lab-made synthetic that just sits there. That was the theory, anyway. I was still skeptical. But my knuckles were cracking. I was desperate.

## What This Pear Tallow Balm Actually Does

So I opened the jar. It’s made in France, which felt fancy for a jar of fat. The texture is… unique. It’s whipped, so it’s not like a greasy lump. It’s this light, almost fluffy cream. You scoop a tiny bit and it melts the second it touches your skin warmth. Not cold, not greasy. Just… melts. Vanishes. My brain was expecting lard. This was not that.

The smell. They said “Pear” and I was worried it would be like a Jolly Rancher or a cheap candle. It’s not. It’s so light. If you shove your nose in the jar, yeah, you get a soft, fresh fruit thing. But on your skin? It’s barely there. A clean, subtle sweetness that fades in a minute. It doesn’t fight with perfume or anything. It’s just nice. Gentle.

I started with my hands. The disaster zone. A pea-sized amount rubbed in and it was gone. No residue. No slick feeling. Just… calm skin. Not instantly magically healed, but just quieter. Less angry. So I got brave. I used it on my face before bed, which felt like the ultimate test. I woke up expecting a grease pit or a breakout. My face just felt… normal. Balanced. Not tight, not shiny. Just normal. That hadn’t happened in years. I kept using it. On my elbows, my knees, my lips when they got chapped. It became my one-jar fix for all the random dry patches spring was throwing at me. The benefits of this tallow skincare thing were suddenly very, very real.

## My Skin After a Few Weeks of This Stuff

I don’t want to sound like an infomercial. But something changed. The flakiness on my cheeks? Gone. The raw, red patches on my hands from washing them a million times a day? Healed. My lips stopped peeling. It’s not a dramatic “look ten years younger” thing. It’s a subtle “your skin just works properly now” thing. It feels resilient. Like it can handle the weird spring weather swings from sunny to windy without freaking out.

I was using like fifteen products before. Now I just wash my face and slap a little of this tallow balm on. Sometimes just that. It’s stupidly simple. I got mine from this small shop on Etsy, which I like because it feels like a person made it, not a factory. The ingredients list is short: grass-fed beef tallow, some oils, natural scent. That’s it. No weird unpronounceable chemicals. After learning about all the natural ingredients, it just makes sense in a way the complicated stuff never did.

Oh, and my cat finally stopped staring at the jar. He’s moved on to judging a houseplant.

## Would I Buy This Beef Tallow Balm Again?

Yeah. I already did. I’m on my second jar. I even got one for my mom, who has psoriasis on her hands. She was even more skeptical than me. “You want me to put cow fat on it?” But she tried it because I begged her. She texted me last week: “What’s in that stuff? My hands don’t itch as much.” That’s a win.

It’s not magic. It’s not going to cure everything. But if your skin is dry, or sensitive, or just being difficult and nothing seems to help? This might. It’s the most effective, simple thing I’ve found. All the tallow skincare benefits, without the fuss. It just… works. I don’t have a better way to say it.

## Quick Questions I Get Asked

**Is beef tallow good for your face?**
Weirdly, yes. Because it’s so similar to our skin’s own oils, it absorbs deeply and helps reinforce your skin’s barrier. It doesn’t just sit on top clogging pores. It’s like giving your skin food it actually knows how to eat.

**Does tallow balm clog pores?**
From everything I’ve read and from my own experience, no. Comedogenic ratings can be misleading. Because tallow mimics sebum, it’s recognized and absorbed. My breakout-prone skin hasn’t had any issues. It actually feels more balanced.

**What does the Pear tallow balm smell like?**
It’s really light and fresh. Not a candy pear. More like the gentle scent of a ripe pear skin, mixed with just a clean, soft sweetness. It’s not strong at all and fades quickly after you apply it. It’s just nice.

Anyway. If you’re curious about this whole grass-fed beef tallow thing, might be worth a shot. My skin’s happy. I’m happy. That’s all I wanted.
